content: The eight elements have been modified to incorporate Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) considerations, as outlined in Box 6. These elements also include guidance for providing recommendations to Ministries following a situational analysis. This approach can be adapted for use at the facility level. Detailed questions addressing these eight elements are provided in Annex 4, Box 6. The eight national planning elements of the National Quality Policy and Strategy (NQPS) handbook, adapted to include WASH, are as follows: 1. Integrate WASH into health sector priorities and/or national quality priorities. 2. Review the national definition of quality and, where applicable, the facility-level definition of quality to assess alignment with WASH. 3. Assess the involvement of WASH stakeholders at both national and facility levels in the development and implementation of the NQPS. 4. Examine available situational analyses to understand the current and historical status of quality work and policy, and identify how WASH can be incorporated. 5. Investigate governance and organizational structures for quality and WASH, as well as the interface between these two areas. 6. Identify methods and interventions being used for quality improvement and determine how WASH is integrated into these interventions. 7. Review the structure of health management information systems (HMIS) and data systems for WASH within quality reporting. 8. For quality indicators and core measures, determine whether data on WASH provision in health services is routinely collected as part of the HMIS. Semi-structured informant interviews are an effective and recognized method for gathering in-depth knowledge and experience within a short timeframe. These interviews provide an opportunity to collect data or information that may not be revealed through desk reviews. Interviews can yield diverse and sometimes conflicting accounts, as expert knowledge is multidimensional and may include interpretative (or explanatory) knowledge derived from subjective experiences, as well as procedural (or process) knowledge. To ensure comprehensive data collection, it is important to conduct a sufficient number of interviews with a range of stakeholders and triangulate the information collected through policy reviews and site visits. There is no fixed number of interviews required; the process may conclude when little or no new information is being obtained. The number of interviews may range from as few as five to as many as fifteen, depending on the context. Interviews should include participants from national and sub-national levels, including healthcare facilities, civil society, private organizations, community members, and facility staff. Box 7 provides a list of stakeholders to consider. It may not be possible to interview everyone due to time constraints or reluctance to engage. At the start of each interview, the aims and objectives of the work should be introduced, focusing on a small number of key points while allowing the discussion to explore unplanned areas. Interviews should be a two-way exchange of information, rather than simply taking participants' time without offering anything in return. In Tajikistan, the interview process involved semi-structured interviews conducted as conversations, guided by a simple list of questions to obtain information on specific topics. The process allowed flexibility in the sequence and focus of questions, in line with the interviewing methodology defined by Kvale. Interviews were limited to one hour and were recorded with the interviewee's consent. The recordings were transcribed for content analysis within predefined dimensions to identify meaning units—contextor content-related words or sentences useful for understanding and comparison. Encouraging stakeholder participation may require building a case for how WASH in healthcare facilities is fundamental to overall quality of care. This case may emphasize health benefits (e.g., fewer infections, prevention of antimicrobial resistance), economic benefits (e.g., reduced healthcare costs, a more productive workforce), or social benefits (e.g., greater dignity for patients and healthcare workers). Tailoring the approach to different audiences may be necessary. Additionally, highlighting the 2019 Resolution, which received unanimous approval from all countries, may underscore the obligation to respond. External support from partners or the opportunity to set an example for other countries may also motivate participation. A comprehensive situational analysis should include facility visits (walk-through infrastructure assessments) to validate monitoring information, service provision data, and the implementation of policies and regulations. These visits provide an opportunity to gather insights from senior management, staff, care seekers, and community groups through on-site structured interviews. Walk-through assessments are not intended to provide formal, statistically rigorous evaluations but should offer an understanding of the services provided and overall conditions. A range of facilities should be visited, including primary healthcare facilities, district and national hospitals, rural and urban facilities, and those using different technologies for water, sanitation, and waste. If WASH coverage data is available, it can be used to select representative facilities for visits. In large countries, achieving geographic diversity may be time-consuming and expensive but should be factored into the budget and timetable to support the development of fair and equitable programs and policies. Including showcase facilities may also help identify inspiring examples and best practices for recommendations. Site visits can be as formal and comprehensive as needed or as time allows. At a minimum, a walk-through of the main patient areas (e.g., outpatient department, maternity, surgery) and infrastructure (e.g., water supply and storage, toilets, hand hygiene facilities, waste storage and treatment areas) is recommended. Using indicators from the WASH FIT assessment template may guide the assessment, but other tools (e.g., local surveys, WASHCON, FACET, IPC facility assessments) can also be used. Photographs may be taken to validate information, but consent must be obtained from the Ministry of Health and/or the facility head at the start of the visit, as well as from any individuals included in the photos. At the end of a visit, the assessment team should meet with the facility manager or administrator to provide feedback on the findings. Specific areas for improvement, major gaps, and strengths should be identified. Providing facility-specific reports with key data following the visit is also important. Data analysis, report preparation, and dissemination should include clear recommendations for further action and follow-up. Results and recommendations may be structured around the eight practical steps, elements of the Resolution, or other national and context-specific priorities derived from the analysis. Regardless of the structure, the results should address the key questions set at the start of the exercise, with each element accompanied by clear recommendations for action, a timeline, responsible organizations or individuals, and a budget.
